title: Anganwadi workers: the first face of the State for a child
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Millions of children, pregnant women and mothers are reached by the ICDS through a woman from their own village.
body:
For millions of rural and urban poor families, the first officer of the State they meet is not a collector or a doctor. She is the Anganwadi worker. She weighs the baby, keeps the register, serves the meal and tells the mother when to go to the clinic. This post looks at the Anganwadi system, the women who run it, the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling on gratuity, and the demands that BMS and other unions have raised.

## Background: ICDS since 1975

The **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** was launched on 2 October 1975. It aims to improve the health, nutrition and early learning of young children and to support mothers. According to standard descriptions of the scheme, it offers:

- supplementary nutrition;
- pre-school (non-formal) education;
- nutrition and health education;
- immunisation;
- health check-ups;
- referral services;
- and, for adolescent girls, counselling.

Children under six, pregnant women, nursing mothers and adolescent girls are the target groups. The centre where all this happens is the **Anganwadi**. The scheme is now delivered under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0. A statement by the Union Minister reported in April 2026 says there are over 14 lakh Anganwadi centres serving nearly 8.9 crore beneficiaries. Funding has been shared between the Centre and States, with the Centre bearing 60 per cent of the allocation in 2018-19, according to one compilation.

## Who runs it

Each centre has an **Anganwadi worker (AWW)** and a **helper (AWH)**. Their work, as described by the Supreme Court in 2022, includes identifying beneficiaries, cooking, teaching at the pre-school level and visiting homes. In practice they:

- keep records and weigh and measure children to track growth;
- give hot cooked meals and take-home rations;
- visit homes of pregnant women and newborns;
- help organise immunisation days and health campaigns in the village;
- enter data using the ICDS Common Application Software and other mobile apps.

During the COVID-19 pandemic they were also asked to support surveys and awareness work. The Government extended a personal accident insurance cover under a special package to Anganwadi and ASHA workers who were in direct contact with COVID-19 patients, subject to conditions, and asked States to provide masks, gloves, soap and sanitisers.

## How they are paid

From 1 October 2018, a worker at a main centre was paid Rs 4,500 a month instead of Rs 3,000, a worker at a mini-centre Rs 3,500 instead of Rs 2,250, and a helper Rs 2,250 instead of Rs 1,500, according to a reply by the Women and Child Development Minister published by PIB. Performance-linked incentives of Rs 500 for workers (from April 2021) and Rs 250 for helpers were added on top. Many States add their own amounts. The Supreme Court judgment mentions reported monthly pay in Gujarat of Rs 7,800 for workers, Rs 3,950 for helpers and Rs 4,400 for mini-centre workers, which shows how much the figure can vary by State.

## The Supreme Court on gratuity

On 25 April 2022, the Supreme Court decided *Maniben Maganbhai Bhariya v. District Development Officer, Dahod*. A Gujarat High Court division bench had held that Anganwadi workers were not "employees" under the Payment of Gratuity Act and that their honorarium was not "wages". The Supreme Court disagreed. Its main points were:

- ICDS is a Central scheme implemented by States, and Anganwadi centres carry out statutory duties under the National Food Security Act, 2013 (nutrition for pregnant and lactating women and children) and pre-primary education for ages three to six under the Right to Education Act;
- the centres are an "extended arm of the Government" and the posts are statutory, so an earlier decision, *State of Karnataka v. Ameerbi* (2007), which had held that these workers did not hold civil posts, was distinguished because the 2013 Act changed the legal position;
- the work is not part-time, given the range of duties;
- the honorarium is wages within the meaning of the Gratuity Act;
- eligible workers are entitled to gratuity with simple interest at 10 per cent a year, and the authorities in Gujarat were directed to act within three months.

Justice Rastogi, in a concurring opinion, said the Centre and States should review working conditions and job security, observing that the honorarium is below minimum wages. The Gujarat Government had argued that the cost would exceed Rs 25 crore. The ruling concerned a Gujarat case, but its reasoning on the Gratuity Act has been applied to other States, such as in a 2024 Tripura High Court decision on Anganwadi centres.

## Common demands

- A higher **honorarium** and its regular payment.
- **Recognition as workers**, not as volunteers.
- **Pension and gratuity** on retirement, and payment of the gratuity that the 2022 judgment recognises.
- Relief from heavy **digital reporting**, or at least proper smartphones and data.
- **Promotion** opportunities, including to supervisor posts.

## The BMS angle

BMS has taken up the cause of scheme workers in representations and demonstrations. At a rally at Jantar Mantar on 11 December 2023, it demanded higher salaries for Anganwadi workers and helpers, their classification as workers in line with the Indian Labour Conference recommendation, social security through EPF, ESI, gratuity and pension, a fair promotion policy and benefits comparable to those of regular Government staff. In its pre-Budget letter of 6 January 2025, BMS said the honorarium should be raised since the last increase was in 2018. BMS argues that these women are part of the nation-building chain that begins with the care of a child in the earliest years, and that the State must recognise their work.

## What remains to be done

Several steps follow from the Court's reasoning. Governments need to implement gratuity where it is due. A pay revision is a live demand, since the last Central increase described here dates from 2018. The Indian Labour Conference's 2013 recommendation on worker status still awaits a decision. And the digital load needs to be matched with training, devices and data.

## A fact to remember

The work is not only data. It is trust. A mother who has not been to a clinic will often listen to the Anganwadi sister, and a village that trusts her is a village where immunisation and nutrition programmes reach children. Any reform that improves her status and pay improves the programme.
